headline: DEA sued by 3 medical cannabis firms over 29 November deadline
dek: Operators in Utah, Arizona and Oklahoma asked the D.C. Circuit on 18 November to halt the DEA's supply-chain deadline before 25 November.
key_points: Standard Wellness Utah, Verde Americano of Arizona and NW Confections OK of Oklahoma filed a petition for review at the D.C. Circuit on 18 November, according to published accounts of the filing.
They challenge the DEA's 30 October notice that tells pending applicants to trade only with other applicants or registrants from 29 November.
The companies want a ruling or an administrative stay before 25 November and say the DEA did not answer their request to suspend the deadline.
Claimed harm includes about $275,900 a month in lost sales in Utah, a 70% workforce cut in Arizona and insolvency in Oklahoma.
body: The DEA's 29 November deadline for medical cannabis supply chains is now in front of a federal appeals court. Three state-licensed operators, Standard Wellness Utah, Verde Americano in Arizona and NW Confections OK in Oklahoma, filed a petition for review at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Wednesday 18 November, according to accounts of the filing published by The Dales Report and The Hype Magazine, both of which build on reporting by Marijuana Moment.

The companies ask the court to rule on the DEA's action, or to issue an administrative stay, before 25 November. That is four days before the date on which the agency says businesses with pending federal applications must buy from and sell to only other applicants and DEA registrants. It is the first court challenge aimed at how rescheduling is being carried out, rather than at rescheduling itself.
## What the companies are challenging

The target is a DEA document dated 30 October and titled DEA Medical Marijuana Timely Applicant Information. As we reported on 19 November, the notice covers businesses that filed complete registration applications between 28 April and 26 June 2026. Under 21 CFR 1301.13(k)(7) these timely applicants may keep operating under their state licences while the DEA reviews them. The notice adds a condition: from 29 November they may deal only with other timely applicants and with registrants, and trading with anyone else could be grounds to deny an application or revoke a registration.

The petition says that condition breaks state markets in a way the agency did not weigh. States ban interstate cannabis commerce, so a grower, processor or dispensary can only trade inside its own state. If too few businesses in a state applied on time, a timely applicant has nowhere else to buy or sell. The filing calls the deadline perfunctory and says it ignores how state markets work, according to The Hype Magazine's account.
## Three legal arguments

The companies make three claims, both outlets report. First, they say the notice contradicts the Justice Department's April rescheduling order and the regulation that followed it. Those texts let timely applicants operate under their state licences while an application is pending. Neither sets a calendar cut-off, and neither ties that permission to the status of a trading partner, the petition argues.

Second, they say the notice is a legislative rule in all but name. It creates new duties, checking partners and rebuilding supply chains on pain of denial or revocation, without the notice-and-comment process that federal law requires for binding rules. The DEA's own document says it does not have the force of law, a point we noted on 19 November; the companies argue it works as law in practice.

Third, they call the notice arbitrary and capricious. The DEA accepted that applicants would need to adjust their supply chains and then gave them 30 days, the petition says, without asking what cutting existing trading relationships would cost or who would bear it.
> The DEA called its notice guidance. The companies' case is that a deadline that can cost a licence is a rule, whatever it is called.
## The harm they describe

The petition puts figures on the damage, as relayed by both outlets. Standard Wellness Utah says it would lose monthly sales averaging about $275,900 after 29 November, along with the suppliers of about 16% of its oil. On our arithmetic that is roughly $3.3 million a year in sales. NW Confections expects its Oklahoma business to become insolvent. Verde expects to cut its workforce by 70%.

The companies say the market has already moved. Utah pharmacies and processors are refusing to deal with non-timely applicants, and one is holding about $80,000 of Standard Wellness product in quarantine, according to The Hype Magazine. Two large Verde customers have asked for proof of its DEA status and a multi-location customer has paused orders. NW Confections has identified 15 dispensary customers, with about 23 locations, that did not apply in time and that it would stop serving.

The petitioners say they asked the DEA directly to suspend the deadline and received no reply. Their argument for speed is that the loss cannot be undone later: in the filing's words, the notice will "sever the supply relationships" each company depends on.
## Where this sits in the wider fight

The lawsuit joins a rollout that state regulators have already criticised. As we reported on 16 November, the Cannabis Regulators Association said the DEA guidance splits most state medical markets into a federal track and a state-only track, and that regulators have had little engagement from the agency. On 12 November we reported that the DEA had sent orders to show cause to medical businesses in several states that also allow adult-use sales. Massachusetts told its licensees on 18 November that it has no federal guidance to give them.

The DEA has registered more than 900 medical dispensaries, mostly in medical-only states, and has published a list of roughly 7,000 timely-applicant locations, The Dales Report notes. A separate, consolidated case in the same court, brought by opponents of reform, challenges the April rescheduling order itself; a request to stay that order was denied, so Schedule III status for state-licensed medical cannabis remains in effect, according to the same outlet.

The three petitioners come from three different kinds of market. Utah is a small, tightly licensed medical programme. Oklahoma has one of the largest numbers of medical licensees in the country. Arizona allows both medical and adult-use sales. That spread is our observation, not a point made in the filing, but it suggests the supply-chain problem is not confined to one model.
## What it means

For operators with pending applications, the practical position has not changed: the 29 November date stands unless the court or the DEA moves it. A business that keeps trading with non-applicants after that date is taking the risk the notice describes. A business that cuts them off is taking the commercial loss now. The petition is, in effect, a request for the court to remove that choice for a time.

An administrative stay is a short, temporary pause that a court can grant while it considers a fuller request. It is not a ruling on the merits. If the court grants one, the deadline would be paused; whether that would cover only the three petitioners or all timely applicants would depend on the court's order. If it declines, the notice applies as written. We have not seen the court's docket, and neither outlet reported a case number.
## What to watch

Watch for any D.C. Circuit order before 25 November, the date the companies asked for. Watch for a DEA response, either in court or as revised guidance. On 29 November the supply-chain deadline takes effect unless something changes. Further out, watch whether other operators or states join the case, and how the court handles it alongside the pending challenge to the rescheduling order itself.
